strengths: First systematic investigation of scaling laws specifically for Diffusion Transformers - fills an important gap in understanding diffusion model scaling
Comprehensive experimental scope with 6 compute budgets (1e17 to 6e18 FLOPs) and models from 1M to 1B parameters demonstrating substantial empirical work
Sound methodology following Hoffmann et al. (2022), with clear validation including accurate prediction at 1.5e21 FLOPs
Multiple convergent evaluation metrics (training loss, validation loss, VLB, exact likelihood, FID) all exhibit consistent power-law trends
Demonstrates robustness across two model architectures (In-Context and Cross-Attention) and two datasets (LAION, COCO)
Clear practical utility for practitioners in computing optimal model/data allocation and predicting generation quality
Thorough documentation with extensive ablation studies (diffusion formulation, EMA, CFG, sampling) and explicit FLOPs counting formulas
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - directly applies Hoffmann et al. (2022)'s approach to diffusion models without technical innovation in the scaling laws framework itself

Critical confounding variable: 1B model uses learning rate decay (1e-4 → 3.16e-5 → 1e-5) while smaller models use constant 1e-4 learning rate, making it difficult to isolate pure scale effects and potentially undermining the 1.5e21 FLOPs prediction reliability
Fixed hyperparameters across all budgets (batch size 1024, optimizer settings constant) - assumption that this only affects coefficients rather than exponents lacks rigorous justification

Significantly limited scope: text-to-image generation only with no exploration of other modalities (video, 3D); single data source (LAION-Aesthetic with LLAVA recaptions); only two model architectures

Weak loss-to-generation-quality connection: FID scaling exponent (-0.234) differs substantially from loss scaling (-0.0273), yet no theoretical explanation provided for why training loss predicts generation quality
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals on power-law coefficients, no R² values, no residual analysis, no significance tests for predictions
Out-of-domain evaluation shows clear vertical offset on COCO with unclear implications for whether scaling exponents themselves are data-dependent
No theoretical insight into why diffusion models follow power laws or how they fundamentally differ from LLMs in scaling behavior

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across a wide range of compute budgets (1e17 to 6e18 FLOPs) with substantial experimental investment
Multiple evaluation metrics (loss, likelihood, FID) all show consistent scaling trends, suggesting robustness of observations
Demonstration that scaling laws generalize to out-of-domain data (COCO) with thoughtful analysis of performance offsets
Extensive ablations on diffusion formulation, EMA coefficient, sampling steps, and architectural variants in appendix
Clear presentation with well-designed visualizations of isoFLOP curves and scaling relationships
First explicit formulation of scaling laws for diffusion transformers (useful characterization even if methodology is known)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: directly applies Hoffmann et al. (2022)'s established methodology to DiT without methodological or conceptual innovation; primarily an engineering contribution rather than scientific insight

Critical validation gap: loss-to-FID connection relies on a single point prediction at 1.5e21 FLOPs (250× extrapolation); FID validation is only on the fitted curve, not independent model evaluation; no uncertainty quantification

Severely constrained experimental setup: fixed hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size) across all budgets; single data regime (Laion-Aesthetic subset); no ablation of how hyperparameter optimization at each scale would change exponents; limits practical applicability
Weak mechanism explanation: no theoretical or empirical justification for why pretraining loss should predict generation quality (FID); many factors beyond loss influence image quality

Limited architectural scope: primarily vanilla transformers with in-context conditioning; cross-attention results limited; only two architectures compared; insufficient to support generalizability claims

Underdeveloped benchmark contribution (Section 4): proposed use of scaling exponents to evaluate model/data quality lacks rigorous validation; only compares two architectures; no evidence that exponent improvements predict actual performance gains

Statistical rigor issues: no R² or fitting diagnostics for parabolic fits; no confidence intervals for power-law exponents; poor fit at 1e17 budget unexplained; stability of loss estimates given EMA smoothing not analyzed
Parabolic isoFLOP assumption not justified: why should diffusion models follow parabolic parameter-loss curves? No sensitivity analysis or ablation of this choice
Non-standard FID computation using CLIP features instead of InceptionV3; makes comparison to other work difficult; FID evaluated on only 10,000 samples
Missing comparisons: related scaling studies (Mei et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024) cited but not quantitatively compared; no comparison to state-of-the-art methods
Narrow scope undermines claims: text-to-image only; claims about other modalities are speculative; findings may not transfer to different data regimes or architectural choices

strengths: First explicit characterization of scaling laws for diffusion transformers, filling an important gap in the literature
Comprehensive experimental coverage across two orders of magnitude of compute budgets (1e17–6e18 FLOPs) with thorough validation
Strong validation strategy: predicting a 1B model's performance at 1.5e21 FLOPs that matches actual training loss, demonstrating practical utility
Multiple evaluation metrics (training loss, validation loss, VLB, exact likelihood, FID) showing consistent scaling trends across metrics
Demonstrates robustness by validating scaling laws on out-of-domain data (COCO) while accounting for dataset-specific differences
Practical application to model/data quality evaluation as a benchmark (Section 4)
Excellent transparency with extensive ablation studies and detailed experimental procedures in appendix
Clear presentation with effective visualizations communicating key findings
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—primarily applies existing scaling law methodology (Hoffmann et al., 2022) to a new domain rather than introducing novel techniques
Narrow experimental scope: restricted to text-to-image generation; other modalities (video, 3D) and broader architectural variants unexplored; dataset limited to single source
Fixed hyperparameters across all scales may introduce systematic bias in scaling exponents; learning rate scheduling differs for the 1B model, potentially affecting generalizability of predictions
Single validation point for major claim (1B model at 1.5e21 FLOPs); extrapolating ~250× beyond observed budgets with only one confirmation point is somewhat risky
Incomplete engagement with concurrent work (Mei et al. 2024, Li et al. 2024)—insufficient discussion of how findings differ from or complement these studies
Limited statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, R² values, or uncertainty quantification for power-law fits; fitting quality not quantitatively assessed
Preliminary benchmarking application (Section 4) supported by only one architectural comparison (in-context vs. cross-attention); claims would benefit from more diverse examples
Insufficient practical guidance: limited interpretation of what scaling exponents mean in practice or how they compare to LLM scaling laws
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; some procedural details (parabola fitting, hyperparameter selection) could be more precisely specified
FID metric limitations underexplored; connection between training loss and FID depends on specific sampling hyperparameters (25 steps, CFG=10.0) with unclear generalization

strengths: First explicit mathematical formulation of scaling laws for diffusion transformers, filling an important gap in the literature
Comprehensive experimental study spanning 6+ orders of magnitude of compute (1e17 to 6e18 FLOPs) with strong validation via training predicted 1B-parameter model at 1.5e21 FLOPs

Robustness demonstrated across multiple dimensions: diverse architectures (In-Context, Cross-Attention, PixArt, Flux), datasets (Laion, COCO, Flickr30k, JourneyDB), metrics (loss, FID, GenEval, human preferences), and resolutions
Extensive ablation studies (12 major ablations) including diffusion formulations, EMA coefficients, CFG scales, and sampling steps, with detailed FLOPs calculations for reproducibility
Practical application demonstrated: scaling laws enable evaluation of model/data quality at reduced computational cost and can distinguish architectural efficiency (in-context vs cross-attention)
Clear presentation with well-organized main paper and comprehensive 24-page appendix providing full experimental details
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: directly applies existing isoFLOP approach from Hoffmann et al. (2022) to diffusion models without developing new theoretical framework or explaining mechanistic reasons why scaling laws hold
Narrow scope limits generalizability: experiments confined to text-to-image synthesis; no evaluation on text-to-video, unconditional generation, or other modalities/tasks

Unclear practical utility of 'predictable benchmark': practitioners still require training multiple models across budgets to fit curves, making computational savings over current practice unquantified

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals on fitted coefficients (Eqs. 7-10), no significance tests for architecture comparisons, power-law fit quality metrics (R², residuals) not reported

Hyperparameter concerns: single hyperparameter set reused across all compute budgets, known source of suboptimality in scaling studies that could introduce systematic bias; poor parabola fit at 1e17 budget unexplained

Large extrapolation uncertainty: main data reaches 6e18 FLOPs but validation at 1.5e21 represents 250× extrapolation; power-law fits can break down at extreme ranges without theoretical justification for when laws should hold

Architecture evaluation undermined by scope: in-context vs cross-attention comparison uses simplified baselines; Appendix J acknowledges modern architectures differ substantially (stronger conditioning, adaptive timestep embeddings, optimized modality interaction), limiting conclusions

Loss-FID correlation lacks mechanistic explanation: paper establishes empirical relationship but does not explain why training loss predicts generation quality or whether this is universal across modalities

strengths: Comprehensive experimental coverage across multiple compute budgets with systematic isoFLOP methodology
Demonstrates consistent power-law scaling across diverse evaluation metrics (loss, VLB, FID, GenEval, human preferences)
Broad validation including multiple architectures, datasets (in-domain and OOD), and resolutions showing robustness
Large-scale validation with 1B-parameter model at 1.5e21 FLOPs provides concrete evidence of predictive accuracy
Extensive documentation with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility and experimental transparency
weaknesses: Limited novelty: paper applies established isoFLOP methodology from LLM scaling law work (Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al.) to diffusion models, confirming expected behavior rather than discovering new principles

Unclear practical utility: proposed use of scaling laws as design benchmark (Section 4) underdeveloped with only one architectural comparison and no demonstrated improvements to actual model design decisions
Narrow scope restricted to text-to-image generation only; generalizability to other modalities and tasks remains unknown, limiting impact for top-tier venue

Weak theoretical connection: loss-to-FID relationship is purely empirical with no mechanistic explanation for why training loss predicts generation quality or what drives the specific scaling exponents
Compute-limited regime only: assumes infinite data throughout; real training becomes data-constrained at scale; finite-data effects relegated to appendix with minimal analysis

Severe extrapolation concerns: 1.5e21 FLOPs represents ~250x extrapolation beyond largest training budget; single large-scale validation point insufficient; no confidence intervals, error analysis, or robustness testing
Statistical rigor issues: no R² values, error bars, or confidence intervals reported; parabola fitting methodology unclear; constant learning rate across budgets introduces potential systematic bias

Architectural comparison potentially misleading: Section J reveals cross-attention's apparent scalability advantage may be artifact of simplified baselines compared to modern in-context designs (MMDiT, Flux) with multiple improvements not tested here

strengths: Addresses a clear gap: First explicit formulation of scaling laws for diffusion transformers, filling an important void left by prior work
Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive range of compute budgets (1e17-6e18 FLOPs), model sizes, metrics, and datasets with rigorous ablations
Strong practical utility: Enables prediction of optimal model/data configurations and serves as a benchmark for evaluating architecture and data quality
Excellent generalization: Validated across out-of-domain datasets, multiple architectures, resolutions, and both data-infinite and data-constrained settings
Technical rigor: Careful FLOPs accounting, proper isoFLOP methodology, stable loss smoothing, and validation on 1B parameter model at 1.5e21 FLOPs
Clear and actionable findings: Precise scaling law equations and demonstration that FID follows predictable power-law trends
Well-presented: Clear organization, high-quality figures, comprehensive appendix, and honest discussion of limitations and related work tensions
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope: Simplified in-context and cross-attention designs don't match state-of-the-art models (Flux, SD3); undermines architectural comparison claims
Restricted modality scope: Limited to text-to-image generation; applicability to video, 3D, image editing, and other tasks unclear
Data-infinite assumption: Most experiments assume data-infinite regime; while ImageNet experiments included, treatment of data-constrained scaling is limited and affects practical applicability
Fixed hyperparameter regime: Same hyperparameters across all compute budgets may introduce systematic bias; unclear if laws reflect architecture properties or suboptimal configurations
Limited methodological novelty: Approach closely follows Hoffmann et al. (2022) for LLMs; isoFLOP and power-law fitting are standard techniques; contribution is primarily empirical

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or sensitivity analysis for fitting methods; parabola fitting robustness not discussed; uncertainty propagation to predictions absent

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Model/data exponent ratio interesting but unexplained; loss-to-FID connection shown empirically but not mechanistically; missing interpretation of why exponents differ from LLM scaling
Limited extrapolation validation: Largest validation at 1B parameters (1.5e21 FLOPs) is reasonable but not extreme; unclear if power-law holds for much larger budgets
